opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the striking thing is that you don't need any exotic philosophical assumptions to make that case. You can just use the standard cost-benefit methods that governments already apply to things like highway safety or environmental regulation, and the numbers come out strongly in favor.

Start with what we just lived through. COVID killed over a million people in the United States alone, and when economists tallied the lost output plus the value of lives lost and health damage, they got estimates on the order of $15 trillion or more for the US. Globally it's many tens of trillions. Pandemics on that scale aren't once-in-a-millennium events either. Historically we see major pandemics every few decades. If you take something like a 1 or 2 percent annual chance of a COVID-scale event, the expected annual cost is hundreds of billions of dollars for the US alone. And that's before you account for the growing risk from engineered pathogens, as biotechnology gets cheaper and more widely accessible. Those could be far worse than anything natural.

Compare that to what the countermeasures cost. Things like metagenomic sequencing to detect novel pathogens early, the ability to scale vaccine production within a hundred days rather than a year, stockpiles of good PPE and elastomeric respirators, research into far-UVC light and better ventilation that could suppress airborne transmission in buildings. Many of these are measured in billions or tens of billions. If they cut the risk or the damage by even a modest fraction, the benefit-cost ratio is something like ten to one, sometimes much higher. That's far better than a lot of what governments routinely fund.

So in my view the puzzle isn't whether it's worth it. It plainly passes the ordinary test that any government agency would apply. The puzzle is why we're not doing it. And part of the answer is political economy. The benefits are diffuse and probabilistic, the costs are concentrated and immediate, and after a crisis passes, attention fades quickly. We saw a burst of interest in 2020 and 2021 and then a lot of the proposed funding got cut or never materialized.

Then, separately, if you do care about the long-term future, the catastrophic tail matters even more. An engineered pandemic that threatened civilization itself would have costs vastly beyond what the standard calculation captures. But I'd emphasize the point I started with: you don't need that argument. Even on a narrow, present-generation, America-first accounting, spending at this scale on pandemic preparedness is a good deal.

r001.rationale: It says expected annual COVID-scale pandemic costs would be hundreds of billions of dollars in the US and endorses preparedness spending at the scale raised in the question, but it does not clearly specify or endorse spending approximately $100 billion every year.

r002.rationale: It describes possible countermeasures and says they could reduce risk or damage, but does not claim that spending hundreds of billions on them would likely have prevented COVID-19.

fable-5.1.text:
Carl Shulman: So the way I'd frame it is the way you'd frame any other big public investment: what's the expected damage you're preventing, and what does it cost to prevent it? And the striking thing about pandemics is that when you actually run those numbers, even with quite conservative assumptions, the case is overwhelming. It's not a close call.

Start with the baseline rate. If you look at the historical record, pandemics that kill on the order of a percent or more of the global population have happened repeatedly: the 1918 flu, the plague pandemics, smallpox in the Americas. Even if you just take the twentieth century, you get several flu pandemics, HIV, and then COVID. Rough estimates put the annual expected mortality from pandemics in the range of hundreds of thousands to millions of lives per year, averaged over time, because most years nothing happens and then occasionally you get something enormous. COVID alone killed something like twenty million people and cost the world economy on the order of ten trillion dollars or more, depending on how you count it.

So if you just do a willingness-to-pay calculation of the kind governments already use for regulations on, say, air pollution or traffic safety, where the US government values a statistical life at around ten million dollars, then the expected annual cost of pandemics comes out in the trillions. A program that cut that risk by even a modest fraction, say ten or twenty percent, would be worth hundreds of billions a year on the same accounting that justifies much more mundane things.

And then on the cost side, the interventions we're talking about are actually fairly well understood. Things like vaccine platforms that can be ready in a hundred days rather than a year, surge manufacturing capacity, metagenomic sequencing to detect novel pathogens early, better ventilation and far-UVC in buildings, stockpiles of high-quality protective equipment. These are tens of billions, not trillions. That's a fraction of what COVID cost in a single month.

The second thing I'd say is that the historical base rate is probably an underestimate going forward, because biotechnology is getting cheaper and more capable, and that means the possibility of engineered pandemics, whether from a state program, a terrorist group, or an accident, is rising over time. That's a tail that doesn't show up in the historical record but which I think dominates the expected harm. And a lot of the same defenses help there too.

The last point is just the politics of it. We spend hundreds of billions a year on defense against threats that are, in expectation, considerably smaller than this. The reason we don't spend it on pandemics isn't that the cost-benefit doesn't work out. It's that the threat is diffuse, nobody's constituency is the one that lives or dies in a given year, and attention fades fast after each crisis, as we saw after COVID. So I'd say the case is extremely strong on the merits, and the real challenge is institutional: building something durable that doesn't get cut the moment the last pandemic recedes from memory.

r001.rationale: It estimates annual pandemic losses in the trillions and says risk reduction would justify spending hundreds of billions per year.

r002.rationale: It describes prevention measures and their costs but does not claim that spending hundreds of billions on them would likely have prevented COVID-19.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate a few different cases. There’s the case based on ordinary pandemics, the case based on very severe pandemics, and then the case based on pandemics that could threaten humanity’s long-term future.

Even the first can justify a lot of spending. If a pandemic causes trillions of dollars of economic damage, then spending hundreds of billions to substantially reduce its probability or severity can be a good deal. And that’s before accounting for the value of the lives saved. But the crucial phrase is “substantially reduce.” The size of the problem doesn’t establish that any particular programme is worth funding.

So I’d want to look at what we’re actually buying. Can we develop the capacity to produce and distribute vaccines much faster? Can we improve detection so that we respond before an outbreak has spread widely? Can we make buildings and protective equipment better at preventing transmission? Those are different investments, with different costs and different degrees of robustness against unfamiliar pathogens.

Then there’s the possibility that advances in biotechnology make deliberately engineered pandemics much more dangerous. That strengthens the case for prevention, but it also changes which interventions you should favour. A system that works well against a familiar natural disease might be much less useful against something designed to defeat it.

And if some of those events could destroy humanity’s future, the potential benefits become much larger still. You don’t need to be confident that such an event is likely to take that seriously. But you do need a credible account of how the spending reduces that risk.

So my answer would be: hundreds of billions is a plausible scale of investment, especially internationally and over a number of years. Whether it’s justified depends on the portfolio of interventions and what additional protection we get at the margin.

r001.rationale: The response calls hundreds of billions over several years a plausible scale and discusses pandemic damage, but does not say the annual actuarial value of pandemic risk justifies about $100 billion per year.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim that spending on pandemic-blocking interventions would likely have prevented COVID-19.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by separating the case for doing much more from the case for any particular spending package. Hundreds of billions is a large amount of money, but pandemics can impose losses measured in trillions, even before you account for deaths and suffering. So you don’t need to eliminate the risk for prevention to be worthwhile. A modest reduction in the probability of a very bad pandemic could justify a substantial investment.

But that doesn’t tell you which investments to make. You want to ask: How much does this particular programme reduce risk? Can we actually deliver it? And what else could we do with those resources? There’s a big difference between funding research that might eventually help and building a capability that reliably gets vaccines or other countermeasures to people quickly.

I’d also distinguish naturally occurring pandemics from deliberately engineered ones. If biotechnology makes it easier to create more dangerous pathogens, historical pandemic frequency becomes a less reliable guide to future risk. That can strengthen the case for prevention, especially measures that work against a broad range of pathogens.

So I think the economic case for spending substantially more is quite strong. The harder question is how much effective prevention we can actually buy, and how quickly we can expand the programmes that deliver it.

r001.rationale: The response says a modest reduction in pandemic risk could justify substantial investment, but it does not judge that annual pandemic risk justifies approximately $100 billion per year.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim that spending on the most promising interventions would likely have prevented COVID-19.
